sources.name: Chronicle
sources.whatIsIt: Narrative accounts of events written by contemporaries — clergy, merchants, court servants.
prompts: Who: Identify the author's religion, social position, and who they were writing for. A court servant sees very different things from a parish priest.
What: Chronicles are narrative accounts — they tell a story, which means they make choices about what to include and how to frame it.
Context: Chronicles tend to reflect the politics of when they were written, not just when the events happened. A chronicle written under Elizabeth carries Protestant assumptions about Mary's reign.
How informed: Were they eyewitnesses, or writing from other accounts? Chroniclers frequently copied from each other and repeated rumour.
Nature: Often written years after events. Memory fades and the political climate changes — both shape what gets written.

sources.name: Ambassador Report
sources.whatIsIt: Letters sent by foreign ambassadors to their governments, reporting on English politics and court affairs.
prompts: Who: The ambassador's nationality determines their priorities. A Spanish ambassador focuses on Habsburg interests; a Venetian on trade and European power. There is no neutral observer.
What: Diplomatic dispatches are written to inform and impress. Admitting uncertainty or missing key events would damage their career.
Context: Ambassadors relied on local informants with their own agendas. 'Popular discontent' may reflect one contact's anxiety, not general opinion.
How informed: Foreign observers often misread English political culture. Being an outsider does not make you more objective.
Nature: Crises are over-reported, stability is under-reported. Ambassadors needed to seem useful to their masters.

sources.name: Government Records
sources.whatIsIt: Documents produced by royal government — Acts of the Privy Council, royal proclamations, parliamentary statutes.
prompts: Who: Whoever dominated the council controlled what got recorded. Somerset's arrest was written down by the men who arrested him.
What: Records decisions, not the arguments and deals behind them. The real politics happened before the clerk picked up his pen.
Context: A proclamation shows what the government intended, not what actually happened. Check local sources to see if it was enforced.
Nature: If something had to be proclaimed, it probably wasn't happening naturally on its own.
How informed: Official records speak in the language of authority — they tell us how the government wanted its actions to appear, not the full reality.

sources.name: Legal Records
sources.whatIsIt: Court proceedings, attainders, and execution records — including the Seymour attainders and Marian heresy trials.
prompts: Who: Charges were constructed by political enemies. Read them as evidence of what those enemies needed people to believe.
What: Tudor treason trials confirmed outcomes already decided. Parliamentary attainder needed no evidence at all.
Context: Somerset's original charges were so weak Northumberland had to retry him on the lesser charge of felony — that tells us something important about the strength of the case.
Nature: Confessions from condemned prisoners were often written by others and read aloud as the price of a less painful death.
How informed: These documents tell us what the government needed people to believe, not what the accused actually did.

sources.name: Churchwarden Accounts
sources.whatIsIt: Parish financial records — spending on church upkeep, buying Bibles, whitewashing images, restoring rood screens.
prompts: Who: Written by local officials doing their administrative duty — not making theological statements.
What: Their value is in their mundanity. Written to record spending, not to persuade. When a parish records whitewashing images, that is real behaviour — not just an intention.
Nature: Never read belief from compliance. A churchwarden who buys a Protestant Bible under Edward and restores a rood screen under Mary is following the law.
Context: They reveal huge regional variation. London looked very different from Cornwall — be careful about national generalisations.
How informed: These are the most direct evidence we have of what actually happened at parish level, rather than what the government wanted to happen.

sources.name: Visitation Records
sources.whatIsIt: Records of bishops inspecting parishes — checking equipment, services, and whether clergy were teaching correctly.
prompts: Who: Written by bishops and their officials — reflects the priorities of church authority, not ordinary parishioners.
What: Standard questions produce standard answers. This creates a false impression of uniformity across very different parishes.
Context: Non-compliance recorded here is some of the best evidence for the gap between what reform intended and what it actually achieved.
How informed: The view from above. Tells us what bishops were looking for, not what ordinary people experienced.
Nature: Most useful when combined with churchwarden accounts and wills. No single local source gives the full picture.

sources.name: Wills
sources.whatIsIt: Legal documents recording last wishes, including religious preambles that can indicate Catholic or Protestant beliefs. Survive in very large numbers.
prompts: Who: A wealthy merchant dictating their own will is a very different source from a labourer whose parish priest wrote it for them. The agency of the testator matters enormously.
What: Their evidential power is statistical, not anecdotal. One will proves almost nothing — hundreds from one area tracked over time can reveal real patterns.
Context: Were testators writing their own words, or repeating phrases the scribe suggested? The two are very different things.
How informed: Most students only see a handful of examples. That is not enough to draw conclusions from.
Nature: Religious preambles can reflect genuine belief, legal convention, or simply whatever formula the local clergyman offered.

sources.name: Edward VI's Chronicle
sources.whatIsIt: Edward VI's personal journal from around 1549 — recording council decisions, rebellions, and religious change in a terse, factual style.
prompts: Who: Written by a boy raised by Protestant humanist tutors. His view of events reflects their values as much as his own.
What: Presented as a private diary — but may have been written to show Edward as an active, capable ruler despite his age.
How informed: After 1549, Edward's information came largely through Northumberland. He is probably repeating Northumberland's version of events without questioning it.
Context: He records Somerset's coming execution with almost no emotion. Reading alongside ambassador reports reveals how much the Chronicle leaves out.
Typicality: Edward never questions Northumberland's actions or the pace and purpose of the Reformation. That absence of doubt is itself revealing.

sources.name: The Devise for the Succession
sources.whatIsIt: A document in Edward's handwriting trying to pass the crown to Lady Jane Grey — altered from 'Jane's male heirs' to 'Jane and her heirs male'.
prompts: Who: Edward was a dying teenager surrounded by powerful men with strong reasons to stop a Catholic succession. Genuine belief and political manipulation are not mutually exclusive.
What: A legal document — but legally impossible. It could not override the 1544 Act of Succession. Tells us about desperation as much as intent.
How informed: Northumberland signed it knowing it would keep him in power. His self-interest shapes the whole document.
Context: Who changed the wording from 'Jane's male heirs' to 'Jane and her heirs male'? Edward, Northumberland's agents, or someone after Edward's death? Never settled.
Nature: The handwriting dispute means we cannot even be certain what Edward himself wrote versus what was added later.

sources.name: The Books of Common Prayer
sources.whatIsIt: Cranmer's Prayer Books — the deliberately vague 1549 version and the clearly Protestant 1552 revision.
prompts: Who: Written by Cranmer, an expert on religious language who knew exactly how to be deliberately ambiguous. Expertise is not the same as objectivity.
What: Official religious texts — telling us what the government wanted people to believe, not how congregations responded.
Context: The 1549 language on the Eucharist was a political calculation — written to keep both Catholics and Protestants on board in a divided country.
Nature: Compare 1549 and 1552 side by side. The removal of almost all Catholic ceremony in 1552 shows how fast the Reformation was actually moving.
How informed: The Western Rebellion was directly triggered by the 1549 Prayer Book. The source and the resistance it caused must be read together.

sources.name: The Edwardian Homilies
sources.whatIsIt: Twelve sermons issued by royal authority in 1547, to be read aloud in churches — written because clergy could not be trusted to preach the new theology themselves.
prompts: Who: Produced by the Edwardian government — an official statement of what the regime wanted every English person to believe.
What: The fact these were needed shows how little the government trusted parish priests in 1547. That itself tells us something important about the state of the clergy.
Context: Far more theologically direct than the 1549 Prayer Book — different documents, different audiences, different strategies.
Nature: Tells us what the government wanted people to believe about salvation and scripture. Not whether they believed it.
How informed: Use visitation records and churchwarden accounts alongside — they show whether the homilies were actually being read in churches.

sources.name: The Zurich Letters
sources.whatIsIt: Letters between English Protestant reformers and theologians in Zurich — especially Heinrich Bullinger — reporting on the English Reformation.
prompts: Who: Committed Protestant reformers writing to their theological heroes abroad. They had every reason to present England positively.
What: Letters between allies — achievements are emphasised, setbacks ignored. They construct the picture of England that reformers wanted Bullinger to see.
Context: Not truly private — writers knew letters could be intercepted. They wrote with that in mind.
How informed: Reformers had real access to events but filtered everything through a Protestant lens that assumed reform was right and necessary.
Typicality: They never question the pace or purpose of the Reformation — only complain it is moving too slowly. That one-sidedness is the point.

sources.name: Kett's Rebellion Articles
sources.whatIsIt: Twenty-nine formal demands from Kett's Rebellion in Norfolk, 1549 — focused on economic grievances like enclosure and excessive rents.
prompts: Who: The careful legal drafting shows this was written by gentry, not ordinary Norfolk peasants. Kett himself was a landowner.
What: Formal written demands — presenting the rebels as loyal subjects with legitimate grievances, not troublemakers.
Context: Shows that ordinary people engaged with national politics in more sophisticated ways than we might expect.
Nature: No religious demands at all. The contrast with the Western rebels' articles is the most important thing about this source.
How informed: The gentry leadership shaped what grievances were articulated. Ordinary rebels may have had different or additional concerns that never made it into the articles.

sources.name: The Western Rebels' Articles
sources.whatIsIt: Demands from the Western (Prayer Book) rebels of 1549 — calling for the Latin Mass, Six Articles, and traditional Catholic practice.
prompts: Who: Written by conservative clergy, not ordinary Cornish and Devon people. The church leadership shaped what this rebellion was about.
What: Formal demands presenting rebels as loyal subjects — but the clergy were using the commons to fight their own battle.
How informed: Many Western rebels didn't speak English and had no opinion on Reformed theology. The clergy were speaking for them — and for themselves.
Context: Compare directly with Kett's Articles. One rebellion is about religion, one about economics. That contrast is central to understanding 1549.
Nature: The rebels called the new Prayer Book 'a Christmas game' — the voice of educated clergy, not ordinary farmers.

sources.name: Commonwealth Writers
sources.whatIsIt: Protestant writers like Robert Crowley and Thomas Lever who attacked enclosure, rack-renting, and the exploitation of the poor in Edward's reign.
prompts: Who: Educated Protestant preachers writing for wealthy, literate audiences — not for the poor they were describing.
What: Moral campaigners, not neutral observers. Their descriptions of poverty are vivid but deliberately shaped to shame the powerful into action.
Context: Writing during a period of real economic hardship — their anger reflects genuine anxiety even if the detail is overstated.
Nature: Protestant social criticism directed upward, toward those with power — not outward toward the commons themselves.
Typicality: They never admit that Protestant religious reform itself might be causing popular unrest. That is a significant blind spot that tells us about the limits of their thinking.

sources.name: Foxe's Acts and Monuments
sources.whatIsIt: John Foxe's martyrology published 1563, recording Protestant persecution under Mary. Under Elizabeth, every parish was ordered to display it alongside the Bible.
prompts: Who: A Protestant exile writing to legitimise his faith by casting its followers as heroic martyrs. Every editorial choice serves that argument.
What: Ordered into every parish under Elizabeth — state-sponsored Protestant propaganda that tells us as much about Elizabeth's reign as Mary's.
Context: Is this a source about Mary's reign, or about how Elizabethan Protestants wanted it remembered? Those are not the same thing.
How informed: Some accounts are second or third hand, already shaped by earlier retellings before they reached Foxe.
Typicality: When Foxe records hostile crowds or difficult deaths, those details are probably accurate — they damage his own argument, so he had no reason to include them.

sources.name: Renard's Diplomatic Dispatches
sources.whatIsIt: Letters from Simon Renard, the Spanish ambassador, to Charles V and Philip II — covering Mary's court, the Spanish marriage, and crises like Wyatt's Rebellion.
prompts: Who: A Spanish diplomat advancing Habsburg interests — not a neutral observer. He highlighted threats and opportunities that mattered to Spain.
What: Diplomatic dispatches written to impress his masters and protect his career. Crises are over-reported, stability ignored.

How informed: Trapped in a Spanish bubble — his contacts shared his anxieties, making him prone to overestimating threats like Wyatt's Rebellion. He also had unusual personal influence over Mary, meaning he was shaping events, not just reporting them.
Context: Repeatedly misread English politics — overestimated the Protestant threat, underestimated noble loyalty to Mary.
Typicality: When he reports something damaging to his own case — like English hostility to Philip — that detail is probably true. He had every reason to leave it out.

sources.name: The Venetian Ambassador Reports
sources.whatIsIt: Diplomatic reports from Venetian ambassadors to the Senate of Venice on Mary's reign and the Spanish marriage.
prompts: Who: Venice had the most professional diplomatic service in Europe — trained observers sent to report accurately, not to advance a dynastic agenda.
What: No stake in English politics — less biased than Renard, but also less well connected to what was really happening at court.
Context: Venice cared about Mediterranean trade and the European balance of power. That shapes what they noticed and what they ignored.
How informed: Most useful when read alongside Renard's dispatches — two observers from opposite sides interpreting the same events very differently. That contrast is the point.
Nature: Professional does not mean infallible. They sometimes applied Italian political thinking to English situations where it didn't fit.

sources.name: The French Ambassador Dispatches
sources.whatIsIt: Reports from French ambassadors — especially Antoine de Noailles — to Henri II, covering the Spanish marriage and English politics.
prompts: Who: French diplomats with a direct interest in destabilising England. Anything that weakened a Spanish-allied England served French interests.
What: De Noailles was in contact with Wyatt's rebels — he was not observing the rebellion, he was helping to cause it.
Context: Most useful when read against Renard's dispatches. Same events, completely opposite agendas — the contrast reveals how national interest shapes what observers claim to see.
How informed: Well connected but deeply partisan. Their reports on English opposition to the Spanish marriage are likely exaggerated.
Nature: French pressure eventually helped drag England into the Habsburg-Valois war and the loss of Calais in 1558. These dispatches are part of that story.

sources.name: Knox's First Blast of the Trumpet
sources.whatIsIt: A pamphlet by Scottish Protestant John Knox, published in Geneva 1558, arguing that female rule was against God, nature, and law. Aimed mainly at Mary I.
prompts: Who: Knox was a powerful, charismatic Calvinist preacher with a zealous congregation behind him. His ideas were widely shared among committed Protestants — this was not just one man's view.
What: A carefully structured theological argument using scripture and classical authorities — designed to be difficult to argue against within the thinking of the time.
Context: Written in Geneva because it could not safely be written in England. What could only be said from abroad tells us about the limits of free expression under Mary.

How informed: Knox was a Protestant exile with strong connections to the reforming network across Europe — well informed about the wider Protestant cause if not always about English politics specifically.
Nature: Backfired badly when Elizabeth became queen — she was furious. This shows Knox was speaking for a committed Calvinist fringe, not mainstream English Protestant opinion.

sources.name: Wyatt's Rebel Documents
sources.whatIsIt: Manifestos and proclamations from Wyatt's rebellion of 1554 — a Kent-based rising against the Spanish marriage.
prompts: Who: Written by rebel leaders trying to build the broadest possible coalition. The language had to be unifying, not divisive.
What: Manifestos are designed to win support — the stated cause was opposition to the Spanish marriage, not Mary's religion. A Protestant rebellion would have attracted far fewer people.
Context: Mary needed it to look like a religious plot to justify her response. Wyatt needed it to look constitutional to maximise support. Both sides had reasons to misrepresent it.
How informed: The rebellion nearly succeeded — Mary only held London after her personal speech at the Guildhall. That near-success shows how fragile her position really was.
Typicality: The documents never mention Protestant motivation — even though it almost certainly existed. That deliberate omission is itself the most important thing about them.
